rv.q: Mantell’s approach is more straightforward, more eager to move us, and ultimately less moving.
Mantell and Battat are able to inject the piece with some hope: hope in the power of collective action, hope that the individual bonds between people might yet be saved.
This world is devised with an unsparing and clear-eyed vision that is startling in its perceptiveness, disheartening in its accuracy and, against all odds, rousingly optimistic in its final moments.
The playwright hasn’t worked out the internal logic of such a world: Much is vague; what few details exist can’t withstand much scrutiny.
I wanted to be shocked and galvanized by the collision of corporate cruelty and human kindness, but Parking Lot peters out in its climactic scenes.

If Mantell’s mournful In the Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot is scarcely a crowd-pleaser, it is a sensitively crafted drama commissioned and produced by Playwrights Horizons, where its world premiere opened Monday.
A tantalizingly dark premise, it proves to be merely drab under the slack direction of Sivan Battat, dulled further by listless performances.

Playwright Sarah Mantell brilliantly reimagined an apocalypse of apathy, in which people knowingly or unknowingly fund and work for a corporation that is, in some way, manufacturing a slow slide in which the coasts of the country slip away and “everybody is looking for somebody” because people are just lost.
The creative team successfully evokes director Sivan Battat’s vision for Mantell’s play.
But like the particular contours of this hellscape, the rest of the characters can seem more of an amorphous blob, a sorority of companions and impromptu therapists and occasional partners in crime.
Just like Amazon, in the end, Mantell’s gripping play delivers.
Mantell's play suffers from poky pacing and schematic storytelling in its attempt to balance quirky romcom and ecological wakeup call.

cn.t: Mantell's climate dystopia about queer warehouse workers living in their cars draws praise for its timely premise and female camaraderie, but critics find the execution underdeveloped, with poky pacing and schematic storytelling undermining its ecological urgency.

vr.q: even though this production feels little undercooked, I'm glad I saw it because I do think it is ripe with potential
